title: Hot surfaces, hot oil and burn prevention on specialty appliances
referencesAtStart: Official references for this lesson: Safe Work Australia, Managing the risks of plant in the workplace (model code of practice) (no date shown). This source has only been partly confirmed for this lesson.
audience: Workers who clean commercial fryers, ovens, dishwashers, steam equipment and other appliances that run hot or hold hot liquids
learningOutcomes: Identify the hot surfaces, hot liquids and steam sources on common specialty appliances
Confirm an appliance is cool enough to clean before starting
Describe the response to a hot oil splash or a suspected oil fire
Apply safe handling for hot trays, racks, filters and doors

instruction.heading: Where the heat is on an appliance
instruction.body: Heat can come from more than one place on a single appliance. A commercial fryer holds hot oil in its vat and may have hot heating elements or gas burners beneath the vat. An oven's door glass, racks, tray runners and cavity stay hot after use, and the door handle can conduct heat. A dishwasher's rinse water, wash arms and internal surfaces can be hot, and steam escapes when the door opens. Coffee machines and steam wands carry hot water and steam. Each of these sources has a different time to cool. Never assume a surface is cool because the display is off. Check it with the back of a hand, or with an approved surface thermometer if the site provides one, and wait until the surface is cool enough to touch safely before you start.

instruction.heading: Oil splashes and oil fires
instruction.body: Hot oil can splash when a basket is lifted, when water is introduced to hot oil, or when a fryer is moved while it still contains oil. Hot oil on skin causes serious burns. If oil splashes on you, cool the skin with cool running water, keep the area covered, and get first aid. The fire response is set by the site's fire procedure and by the appliance's own fire protection, such as a suppression system fitted over the fryer or hood. Do not disturb, disconnect or cover a fire suppression system or its nozzles during a clean. Your business must record the extinguisher type and the site fire procedure in the safety field before you clean any fryer. Do not use water on a burning fryer or a burning oil pan.

instruction.heading: Safe handling of hot parts and steam
instruction.body: Hot trays, racks, filters and doors need the right gloves and a safe handling method. Use heat-resistant gloves rated for the task, check the gloves for holes before you use them, and handle parts only when they are cool enough for the gloves to be safe. Do not lean over a hot appliance when you open a door, because steam can escape. Open the door slowly, stand to one side, and let the steam clear before you put your face or hands close. Use a damp cloth and let the surface cool. Keep flammable materials, such as paper, cloths and aerosol cans, well away from hot surfaces and never leave a damp cloth or towel on a hot element. Do not spray cold water onto a hot oven door glass.

procedure: Before the job, check the appliance's status, and confirm with the site contact whether it has been used in the last period and whether it still holds oil or hot water.
Check each surface you will touch with the back of a hand or an approved thermometer, and wait until it is cool enough to touch safely.
Confirm the fire response for the appliance from the site fire procedure, and confirm where the extinguisher or fire blanket is.
Put on the heat-resistant gloves rated for the task, and check them for damage before use.
Open oven and dishwasher doors slowly and to the side, and wait for steam to clear before you reach in.
Handle hot trays, racks and filters only after they have cooled enough for safe handling. Keep them on a stable, heat-resistant surface.
Never use water on hot oil or on a fryer fire. If a fire or splash occurs, follow the site fire procedure, call for help, and treat any burn with cool running water.
Record any burn, splash, fire or heat-related incident, and report it to the site contact and the business's incident reporting procedure.

workedExamples.situation: A commercial fryer is booked for an external clean at the end of a busy lunch. The top of the vat looks cool, but the control panel is still lit on a warm-up setting.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you start wiping the fryer straight away?
workedExamples.reasoning: The fryer is not safe to clean yet. The control panel indicates the appliance is still active, and oil stays hot for a long time. Do not start. Wait until the site contact confirms the fryer is off and the oil has cooled to a safe level under the site procedure, and check the surfaces you will touch. Only then start the external clean, keeping away from the oil vat and any hot element.

workedExamples.situation: You open the door of a commercial oven and a cloud of steam comes out. Your gloved hand is close to the door handle, and the wet cloth in your other hand is on the floor.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should you change in how you work?
workedExamples.reasoning: Steam burns can happen when a door is opened quickly. Step to one side, open the door slowly, and wait for the steam to clear before you reach in. Keep the wet cloth off the floor where it can slip, and keep it away from the hot door glass. Do not spray the glass with cold water. Record the event if any steam reached you.

equipmentAndPpe: Heat-resistant gloves rated for the task, checked for damage before each use
Eye protection and a non-slip footwear for the wet and oily floor
Approved surface thermometer, if the site provides one
Site fire extinguisher or fire blanket, located and recorded before work starts

commonErrors.error: Judging a surface cool by its appearance or by the display being off.
commonErrors.prevention: Check with the back of a hand or an approved thermometer, and wait until the surface is cool enough.

commonErrors.error: Pouring water on a fryer fire or on hot oil.
commonErrors.prevention: Never use water on hot oil or a fryer fire. Follow the site's fire procedure and call for help.

commonErrors.error: Spraying cold water onto a hot oven door glass to speed up cooling.
commonErrors.prevention: Let the glass cool naturally, and use a damp cloth only once it is cool enough.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Hot oil and steam burns can be serious. Treat any burn with cool running water and seek first aid, and record the incident.
Do not disturb suppression nozzles or detection devices.

This lesson does not grant any authority to service or modify fire protection equipment. The plant model code treats appliances as plant, so the duty to manage risk applies to the cleaning work (no page date shown).

qualityStandard: Each surface is confirmed cool enough to touch before it is cleaned
No water is used on hot oil or on a fryer fire
Fire protection equipment is left in place and undisturbed
documentationEvidence: The check of surface temperature, or the reason the appliance was left until cool
The fire response details for the site, including extinguisher and blanket location
Any burn, splash or steam incident, with the first aid given and the report made
summary: Heat sources include oil, elements, burners, door glass, racks and steam, and each cools at a different rate.
Never use water on hot oil or a fryer fire. Follow the site fire procedure.
Open doors slowly, use rated gloves, and wait until surfaces are cool enough before cleaning.

knowledgeChecks.question: A fryer's control panel is still lit on a warm-up setting after lunch. What should you do before cleaning?
options: Start cleaning the top of the vat, since it looks cool to the touch and the heating element has probably switched off
Pour cold water into the vat to speed up cooling, so the cleaning can start sooner and the crew can finish
Wait until the site contact confirms the fryer is off and the oil has cooled to a safe level under the site procedure
Lift the basket to check the oil temperature by feel, since the basket shows how hot the oil still is

knowledgeChecks.question: A fryer catches fire during a clean. Which response is correct?
options: Pour water on the fire to put it out quickly, since water cools the oil and stops the flames fast
Open the vat and stir the oil so the flames can be seen, then put them out with the nearest tool
Disconnect the fire suppression nozzles so the fire is not affected by the spray and can burn out
Follow the site fire procedure, use the fire protection the site provides, and never use water on the oil fire

knowledgeChecks.question: How should you open an oven door that has just been used?
options: Slowly, standing to one side, and waiting for steam to clear
Fully and quickly, standing in front of it so the steam hits you
By pulling hard on the glass panel of the door to open it
After spraying the door with cold water to reduce the steam

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is oil more hazardous than water for holding heat?
options: Oil does not hold heat at all, so it cools as soon as it is removed from the element
Oil holds heat for longer, so a surface that looks cool may still be hot below the surface
Oil is always colder than water, which means a vat of oil is always safe to touch
Oil cannot be seen in the vat, so it is hard to tell whether it is hot or cold

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should you avoid spraying cold water onto a hot oven door glass?
options: The cold water will make the door heavier
Cold water will remove the glass coating
The rapid temperature change can crack the glass
Cold water will turn the oven on again
